summaries.summary: LSTM units BIBREF1 are popular for sequence modeling and language modeling, but their input and context vectors receive simple linear transformations before gating.
Increasing input and context vector dimensions can improve expressiveness but raises parameters and may limit generalizability, as Figure FIGREF1 shows for LSTMs.
The Pyramidal Recurrent Unit (PRU) uses pyramidal transformation (PT) for input vectors and grouped linear transformation (GLT) for context vectors.
PRUs improve language modeling perplexity by up to 1.3 points, reaching 56.56 and 64.53 on Penn Treebank and WikiText2 with 15-20% fewer parameters.
The paper first describes methods with gating structures and transformations for improving RNNs, then reviews recent language modeling work.
Pyramidal Recurrent Units (PRUs) improve context modeling with higher dimensional vector representations while learning fewer parameters, as overviewed in Figure FIGREF2.
The basic transformation in many recurrent units is a linear transformation INLINEFORM0 defined as DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 are learned weights that linearly map INLINEFORM1 to INLINEFORM2, and biases are omitted.
Motivated by sub-sampling in computer vision, the input vector INLINEFORM0 is subsampled into INLINEFORM1 pyramidal levels with scale-specific transformations INLINEFORM6.
INLINEFORM0 indicates concatenation, and pyramidal transformation with INLINEFORM1 is the same as the linear transformation.
An element-wise sum combines input and output when dimensions match to produce a residual analog of pyramidal transformation, as shown in Figure FIGREF2 BIBREF25.
The input vector INLINEFORM0 is sub-sampled into INLINEFORM1 pyramidal levels using the kernel-based approach BIBREF8, BIBREF9 with kernel INLINEFORM2.
INLINEFORM0 represents the stride and INLINEFORM1.
Pyramidal transformation with INLINEFORM0 pyramidal levels reduces linear transformation parameters by a factor of INLINEFORM5, with INLINEFORM8 fewer parameters in an example.
Differing semantics of dense word embedding input vectors and highly contextualized context vectors motivate their separate treatment in the PRU architecture.

Grouped linear transformation (GLT) is proposed for recurrent connections to improve generalization and enable high dimensional representations, with Section SECREF39 suggesting GLTs are more effective.
A GLT splits input vector INLINEFORM3 into INLINEFORM4 smaller groups, applies linear transformation INLINEFORM6 to each, and concatenates INLINEFORM10 outputs into INLINEFORM12.
GLTs learn low-dimensional representations, require INLINEFORM0 fewer parameters than linear transformations, and equal linear transformations when INLINEFORM1.
The Pyramidal Recurrent Unit (PRU) extends the basic gating architecture of LSTM with pyramidal and grouped linear transformations.
At time INLINEFORM0, the PRU combines input vector INLINEFORM1 and previous context vector INLINEFORM2 using a transformation function DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 indexes gates in the LSTM model, while INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 represent pyramidal and grouped linear transformations from EQREF10 and EQREF15.
A PRU cell incorporates INLINEFORM0 into LSTM gating architecture, taking INLINEFORM2, INLINEFORM3, and INLINEFORM4 to produce gate signals, context vector INLINEFORM9, and cell state INLINEFORM10.
INLINEFORM0 is element-wise multiplication, INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are sigmoid and hyperbolic tangent activations, and LSTM is a PRU special case when INLINEFORM3 = INLINEFORM4 =1.
The PRU is evaluated on two standard word-level language modeling datasets, compared with state-of-the-art methods, and examined in detail.
Experiments use Penn Treebank (PTB) BIBREF28 prepared by BIBREF29 and WikiText2 (WT-2) BIBREF20 with splits from BIBREF0.
AWD-LSTM BIBREF0 is extended with 3-layers of PRU, embedding size of 400, model size fixed to 19M, hidden sizes 1000, 1200, and 1400, and word-level perplexity.
Regularization experiments use Standard dropout with probability of 0.5 and Advanced dropout with techniques and values from BIBREF0, called AWD-PRU.
Table TABREF23 compares the PRU with state-of-the-art methods and shows the PRU achieves the best performance with fewer parameters.
PRUs match or outperform LSTMs, improving with increasing INLINEFORM0 and outperforming LSTMs by about 4 points on PTB and about 3 points on WT-2 at INLINEFORM1.
Advanced dropouts improve PRUs by about 4 points on PTB and 7 points on WT-2, with finetuning adding about 2 points on PTB and about 1 point on WT-2.
With standard dropout, the PRU outperforms most state-of-the-art methods on PTB, and with advanced dropouts improves perplexity by about 1 point while learning 15-20% fewer parameters.
With dynamic evaluation on the PTB test set, PRU perplexity improves from 62.42 to 55.23 while LSTM perplexity improves from 66.29 to 58.79.
The PRU learns higher-dimensional representations with more generalization power, and analysis reveals factors explaining its language modeling gains.
Using 3687 contexts from the PTB validation set and bins of size 0.23, the PRU more often produces lower entropy next-token distributions than the LSTM.

The pyramidal transform models words at different resolutions, with pyramid level 1 embeddings showing higher variance than LSTM across all POS categories and pyramid level 2 showing extremely low variance.
Saliency analysis shows PRUs give more relevance to contextual words and better gradient coverage than LSTMs, with BIBREF0 converging in 500 epochs with PRU and 750 with LSTM.
Ablations use standard dropouts, a single PRU layer, embedding and hidden layer size 600, and word-level perplexities on PTB and WT-2 validation sets.
The number of pyramidal levels INLINEFORM0 and groups INLINEFORM1 control the trade-off between performance and number of parameters in PRUs.
Increasing pyramidal levels INLINEFORM2 at fixed INLINEFORM3 drops PRU performance by about 1 to 4 points while reducing recurrent unit parameters by up to 15%.

Varying INLINEFORM2 at fixed pyramidal levels INLINEFORM3 significantly decreases recurrent unit parameters with minimal perplexity impact, including 77% fewer parameters and about 12% higher perplexity.
Table TABREF43 shows pyramidal transformation for input vectors improves perplexity by about 1 point on PTB and WT-2 while reducing recurrent unit parameters by about 14%.
Sub-sampling kernel INLINEFORM0 with stride INLINEFORM1 and size of 3 is set using Skip, Convolution, Avg. pool, and Max pool.
Table TABREF45 shows average pooling performs best, skipping is comparable, convolution-based sub-sampling underperforms averaging, and max pooling performs poorly.

The Pyramidal Recurrent Unit improves language modeling perplexity across settings, improves gradient flow and expands the word embedding subspace, with future work planned on other tasks and inference techniques.
